opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it feels very different, and I think that difference matters more than people realize.

When we worked on the Transformer, there wasn't a big top-down mandate. It came out of a lot of freedom. People at Google Brain could follow their curiosity, chat over lunch, and wander into each other's projects. Nobody told us to build a new architecture to replace RNNs. A group of us found the idea interesting and kept pulling on the thread. There wasn't enormous pressure to publish or ship something by a specific date, and that gave us room to try things that might not have worked.

Now the field is a victim of its own success. There's so much money, attention and competition that a lot of research has become very exploitative rather than explorative. Everyone is working on roughly the same thing, the same architecture, the same scaling recipe, and squeezing out another half a percent on a benchmark. If you're a PhD student or a researcher at a big lab, the safe move is to do something incremental on top of Transformers, because if you go off and try something really different, you risk being scooped or looking unproductive for a year.

I find that a bit ironic, and I've said publicly that I'm getting a bit sick of Transformers. Not because they're bad. They obviously work incredibly well. But I worry that because they work so well, we've stopped looking for the next thing. There may be something much better out there that nobody is finding because all the talent and compute is concentrated in one basin.

That's a big part of why I wanted to start Sakana. I wanted to deliberately recreate some of those original conditions: give smart people freedom, let them follow what they find interesting, and take inspiration from things like evolution and nature rather than just making the model bigger. I think the next breakthrough is more likely to come from that kind of environment than from a thousand people optimizing the same recipe.

r001.rationale: The response says today’s pressure makes researchers favor incremental Transformer work, while reduced freedom to explore may keep the next breakthrough from being found.

r002.rationale: It describes the Transformer’s development as arising from researchers’ curiosity and collaboration, with no top-down mandate to create a replacement for RNNs.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's quite different, and not entirely in a good way. When we were working on the Transformer at Google, there was a lot of slack in the system. Nobody was really watching us too closely. We were a small group of people who happened to find each other, wandering between desks, arguing on whiteboards, and we were allowed to just try things. There was no sense that this was a race, or that if we didn't publish in the next six weeks someone else would scoop us. The expectations were low, which paradoxically gave us a lot of freedom.

Compare that to now. The field has become incredibly crowded and incredibly fast. Everyone is trying to beat the same benchmarks, chase the same scaling curves, and squeeze out another point on the same leaderboards. There's a huge amount of pressure, both commercial and academic, and that pressure pushes people toward incremental, safe work. If you're a young researcher today, taking a year to explore some weird idea that might not pan out is genuinely risky for your career. That's exactly the kind of exploration that produced the Transformer in the first place.

I also think there's a kind of monoculture forming. Because the Transformer works so well, almost all the energy goes into it. That's rational in the short term, but I worry about it. The Transformer wasn't the end of history. It was one idea among many that happened to be a good fit for the hardware at the time. It would be a shame if we stopped looking for the next one because this one is good enough.

That's part of why I ended up co-founding Sakana. I wanted to recreate some of that environment where people have room to be curious, to explore nature-inspired ideas and strange directions without the constant pull of the next product release. I don't want to be too romantic about the old days, because there was a lot of luck involved too. But I do think the conditions matter, and right now the conditions are optimised for speed rather than for surprise.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the freedom to explore that produced the Transformer with today’s pressure for fast, incremental work, which puts exploratory breakthroughs at risk.

r002.rationale: It describes a small group that found one another and tried ideas freely, with little oversight or pressure, conveying bottom-up development rather than a top-down plan.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot more pressure now. When we were working on the Transformer, we had room to follow an idea because it was interesting, without necessarily knowing where it would lead. It wasn’t, “We need to build the thing that’s going to transform the industry.” We were trying to make something work, and we could experiment.

Now, with so much attention and money involved, there’s a temptation to make research much more directed: here’s the roadmap, here’s the benchmark, here’s what we need to ship. That’s understandable, but I worry that it squeezes out the kind of exploration that produces something unexpected. If you already know what the result is supposed to look like, you’re limiting what you can discover.

You still need people who can spend time on an idea that sounds a bit odd, try it, find out it doesn’t work, and learn something. Having more resources is fantastic, but having the freedom to use some of those resources without a guaranteed payoff matters too.

r001.rationale: The response says today’s pressure and directed roadmaps can squeeze out the exploratory freedom that may produce unexpected breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: It describes Transformer work as following an interesting idea and experimenting, rather than building to a predetermined industry-changing goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is how much pressure there is now to know what a piece of research is going to produce before you do it. If you’re committing a huge amount of compute, people quite reasonably want a predictable return. But that can make it harder to try something that sounds a bit strange, or that might simply fail.

When we were working on the Transformer, we had room to explore. It wasn’t a grand plan where we knew attention was going to underpin this enormous industry. We were trying things, discussing what wasn’t working, and following ideas that seemed interesting. Looking back, it’s easy to make that process sound much more inevitable than it felt.

There’s obviously far more excitement and more resources now, which is fantastic. But I think you have to deliberately protect the freedom to pursue an idea before you can justify it with a benchmark or a business case. Otherwise, you get very good at improving the thing you already know works, and perhaps less good at finding the next thing.

r001.rationale: The response says current pressure makes unusual or potentially unsuccessful research harder and may hinder finding the next idea, but it does not clearly connect diminished freedom to a lower likelihood of a Transformer-like breakthrough.

r002.rationale: The response says the Transformer was not guided by a grand plan and describes trying things, discussing problems, and following interesting ideas.
